tagline: A river road winds through rain forest and weathered seafloor cliffs
intro: The Nestucca River Back Country Byway follows a wooded canyon through Oregon’s Coast Range. The Bureau of Land Management describes a slow, winding route beside the river, with four riverside campgrounds. The Federal Highway Administration gives its length as 48 miles and advises allowing an hour and a half to drive it.

The canyon walls expose seafloor sandstone and basalt, now weathered and covered in lichens, worts and mosses. Annual rainfall of 120 inches sustains the temperate rain forest. The Nestucca drains a timber-producing part of the Coast Range, and log trucks may be encountered on the byway throughout the year.

From Beaver on U.S. 101, Blaine Road reaches the byway after seven miles. Follow the river inland, passing the Alder Glen recreation site along the corridor. On the Carlton side, Meadow Lake Road connects town with the byway twelve miles to the west.
notice: Weathered sandstone and basalt cliffs carry lichens, worts and mosses.

moments.title: Beaver
moments.text: Beaver sits beside both U.S. 101 and the Nestucca River, where the approach to the byway leaves the coast highway. Its post office was established in 1889. From here, the river continues southwest past Hebo and Cloverdale before entering Nestucca Bay at Pacific City. The drive toward Carlton goes inland instead, taking Blaine Road seven miles to the byway.

moments.title: Alder Glen
moments.text: Alder Glen places a waterfall beside a campground on the Nestucca. Alder Glen Falls can be seen from a campsite in late winter; spring views include both the falls and the Nestucca River. Alder Glen is one of four BLM campgrounds along the road, together with Dovre, Fan Creek and Elk Bend. The surrounding byway follows a canyon of sandstone and basalt cliffs beneath temperate rain forest.

moments.title: Carlton
moments.text: Carlton grew beside the railroad after an earlier post office and stagecoach stop had served the area from farther west. Wilson Carl’s Mountain House, about seven miles west of town, combined the post office, stagecoach stop and blacksmith shop. The railroad built on the Carlton side because crossing the mountain to Carl’s property was not feasible. A post office opened in Carlton itself in 1874, with F.J. Fryer as its first postmaster.
